hook.text: The Airbnb host says the guest broke a lamp. The guest denies it. Who does the platform believe?

buildup.text: Dispute resolution is a marketplace acting as judge, jury, and enforcer between two sides.

discovery.text: Amazon almost always sides with the buyer. This builds buyer trust but frustrates sellers.

twist.text: Some sellers abuse this. 'Return fraud' costs Amazon $27 billion/year—buyers return used items as new.

climax.text: Dispute systems reveal a platform's true values: who does it protect when conflicts arise?

punchline.text: Buyer or seller? The platform picks a side. Every marketplace does.

quiz.question: Who does Amazon typically favor in disputes?

details.summary: Marketplace dispute resolution handles conflicts between buyers and sellers over quality, delivery, payments, and misrepresentation. Effective dispute resolution builds trust in the marketplace by ensuring both parties have recourse.
details.whyItMatters: Dispute resolution is the safety net that makes marketplace commerce possible. Without reliable conflict resolution, buyers fear fraud and sellers fear chargebacks..
takeaways: Dispute resolution handles conflicts over quality, delivery, and payment issues
Consistent and fair processes build trust for both buyers and sellers on the platform
Bias toward either side creates imbalance that damages marketplace health

faq.question: How do major marketplaces handle buyer-seller disputes?
faq.answer: Most start with automated resolution based on tracking data and policy rules. Unresolved cases escalate to human review teams. Amazon's A-to-Z guarantee automatically sides with buyers in most cases. eBay uses a structured resolution process with escalation to eBay decision makers as the final step.

faq.question: Why do some marketplaces have a reputation for siding with buyers?
faq.answer: Protections that favor buyers reduce purchase anxiety and increase transaction volume. Platforms calculate that losing some seller transactions is less costly than losing buyer confidence..
